findings.explanation: high confidence. In sentence [p4-6], the authors define an automorphism $\varphi$ of $H$ by choosing a non-trivial automorphism of $\text{span}\{x_i\}_{i<n}$ and setting $\varphi(y) = y$ for all $y \in Y$. However, $H$ is not the internal direct sum of $\text{span}(Y)$ and $\text{span}\{x_i\}_{i<n}$, so this map is not well-defined unless $\text{span}(Y) \cap \text{span}\{x_i\}_{i<n} = \{0\}$ (or $\varphi$ fixes their intersection pointwise). Since $U \subseteq \text{span}(Y)$, $\text{span}(Y)$ contains the subgroup $\langle U \rangle$ generated by $U$. In any connected Boolean Polish group (such as $L^0([0, 1], \mathbb{Z}_2)$ with symmetric difference), any open neighborhood $U$ of the identity generates the entire group, so $\text{span}(Y) = G$ and $\text{span}\{x_i\}_{i<n} \subseteq \text{span}(Y)$. Consequently, any linear map fixing $Y$ pointwise must fix all of $\text{span}(Y) = G$, so it cannot act non-trivially on $\text{span}\{x_i\}_{i<n}$, making the definition of $\varphi$ impossible. Witness: For a finite counterexample: In $G = (\mathbb{Z}_2)^4$, let $L = \text{span}\{e_1, e_2\}$ and $U = \{0, e_3, e_4, e_1 + e_3 + e_4\}$. Then $U$ satisfies the conditions of Lemma 2.3, and $Y = \{e_3, e_4, e_1 + e_3 + e_4\} \subset U$ is linearly independent and spans $U$. But $e_1 = e_3 + e_4 + (e_1 + e_3 + e_4) \in \text{span}(Y) \cap L$. Any linear map fixing $Y$ pointwise must fix $e_1$, so an automorphism of $L$ swapping $e_1$ and $e_2$ cannot be extended to $H = \text{span}(Y \cup L)$ by setting $\varphi(y) = y$ on $Y$.
